claim: Coronary heart disease is the leading cause of mortality worldwide, causing 7.4 million deaths in 2015.
source: Coronary heart disease is the leading cause of mortality worldwide, causing 7.4 million deaths in 2015.
evidence: This is a factual statement about mortality statistics that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention does not guarantee reperfusion of the downstream capillaries supplying the myocardium.
source: To treat cardiac ischaemia, primary percutaneous coronary intervention is used to re-open the culprit coronary artery, but this does not guarantee reperfusion of the downstream capillaries supplying the myocardium (Krug et al., 1966; Kloner et al., 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Krug et al., 1966; Kloner et al., 1974).

claim: No-reflow affects up to 50% of patients.
source: A lack of capillary reperfusion - 'no-reflow' - affects up to 50% of patients (Niccoli et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Niccoli et al., 2009.

claim: No-reflow predicts a raised prevalence of deleterious complications including congestive heart failure, malignant arrhythmias and cardiac death.
source: A lack of capillary reperfusion - 'no-reflow' - affects up to 50% of patients (Niccoli et al., 2009), and predicts a raised prevalence of deleterious complications including congestive heart failure, malignant arrhythmias and cardiac death (Niccoli et al., 2009; Wu et al., 1998; Morishima et al., 2000; Ørn et al., 2009; Kloner, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: No-reflow has been attributed to swollen endothelial cells and/or cardiomyocytes compressing the lumen of capillaries.
source: No-reflow has been attributed to swollen endothelial cells and/or cardiomyocytes compressing the lumen of capillaries (Kloner, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kloner, 2011.

claim: No-reflow has been attributed to leukocytes adhering to and plugging capillaries.
source: No-reflow has been attributed to swollen endothelial cells and/or cardiomyocytes compressing the lumen of capillaries (Kloner, 2011), or to leukocytes adhering to and plugging capillaries (Engler et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engler et al., 1983.

claim: Depleting blood of granulocytes reduces no-reflow.
source: However, although depleting blood of granulocytes reduces no-reflow (Engler et al., 1986)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Engler et al., 1986.

claim: Leukocyte adhesion to capillaries in reperfused hearts is modest compared to the adhesion seen in post-capillary venules.
source: leukocyte adhesion to capillaries in reperfused hearts is modest compared to the adhesion seen in post-capillary venules (Habazettl et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Habazettl et al., 1999.

claim: No treatment exists for coronary no-reflow after decades of investigation.
source: No treatment exists for coronary no-reflow after decades of investigation, even though it predicts a worse outcome after myocardial ischaemia (Niccoli et al., 2009; Wu et al., 1998; Morishima et al., 2000; Ørn et al., 2009; Kloner, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations indicating the clinical significance of no-reflow and the lack of effective treatments.

claim: In the brain and retina, blood flow is partly regulated by contractile pericytes located on capillaries.
source: In the brain and retina, blood flow is partly regulated by contractile pericytes located on capillaries (Hirschi and D'Amore, 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hirschi and D'Amore, 1996.

claim: Brain and retinal pericytes respond to vasoactive messengers released from active neurons and astrocytes by altering their tone, thus altering capillary diameter and blood flow.
source: In the brain and retina, blood flow is partly regulated by contractile pericytes located on capillaries (Hirschi and D'Amore, 1996), which respond to vasoactive messengers released from active neurons and astrocytes by altering their tone, thus altering capillary diameter and blood flow (Peppiatt et al., 2006; Puro, 2007; Hall et al., 2014; Biesecker et al., 2016; Duan et al., 2016; Kisler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Ischaemia, spinal cord injury and epilepsy lead to a contraction of pericytes, causing constriction of capillaries.
source: Furthermore, ischaemia, spinal cord injury and epilepsy lead to a contraction of pericytes, causing constriction of capillaries (Hauck et al., 2004; Peppiatt et al., 2006; Yemisci et al., 2009; Hall et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017; Leal-Camanario et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: After ischaemia, pericyte contraction is followed by the pericytes dying in rigor which hinders subsequent capillary dilation.
source: Furthermore, ischaemia, spinal cord injury and epilepsy lead to a contraction of pericytes, causing constriction of capillaries (Hauck et al., 2004; Peppiatt et al., 2006; Yemisci et al., 2009; Hall et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017; Leal-Camanario et al., 2017), and for ischaemia this is followed by the pericytes dying in rigor (Hall et al., 2014) which hinders subsequent capillary dilation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hall et al., 2014.

claim: Pericytes exist in the heart.
source: Pericytes also exist in the heart (Tilton et al., 1979)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tilton et al., 1979.

claim: Pericytes are the second most numerous cell type in the heart after endothelial cells.
source: Pericytes also exist in the heart (Tilton et al., 1979), where they are the second most numerous cell type after endothelial cells (Nees et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nees et al., 2012.

claim: Only 1 in 5000 cardiac papers in PubMed mentions pericytes.
source: They are poorly understood (only 1 in 5000 cardiac papers in PubMed mentions pericytes)
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the literature that can be verified from PubMed database searches.

claim: It is debated whether cardiac pericytes are contractile.
source: They are poorly understood (only 1 in 5000 cardiac papers in PubMed mentions pericytes): it is debated whether they are contractile (Tilton et al., 1979; Joyce et al., 1985)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to conflicting or uncertain prior research.

claim: Attention on cardiac pericytes has focused on possible functions including angiogenesis, immune defence, haemostasis and cardiac regeneration.
source: it is debated whether they are contractile (Tilton et al., 1979; Joyce et al., 1985) and attention has focused on other possible functions for them including angiogenesis, immune defence, haemostasis and cardiac regeneration (Nees et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nees et al., 2013 and Chen et al., 2015.

claim: The left ventricular coronary capillary bed comprises an array of parallel capillaries linked by occasional connector capillaries running roughly orthogonal to the main direction of flow.
source: The left ventricular coronary capillary bed comprises an array of parallel capillaries linked by occasional connector capillaries running roughly orthogonal to the main direction of flow (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A which shows the capillary architecture.

claim: The great majority of coronary capillaries are contacted by pericytes.
source: Labelling capillaries with FITC- or Alexa647-isolectin B4, and pericytes in rat with antibody to NG2 (Figure 1A) or PDGFRβ (Figure 1C), or in mouse with transgenic expression of DsRed under the NG2 promoter (Figure 1C), showed that the great majority of coronary capillaries were contacted by pericytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A and 1C.

claim: Pericytes differ from vascular smooth muscle cells in that their somata are spatially separated along the capillary, located either with a bump-on-a-log appearance on the straight parts of capillaries, or at the branch points of capillaries.
source: Pericytes differ from vascular smooth muscle cells in that their somata are spatially separated along the capillary, located either with a bump-on-a-log appearance on the straight parts of capillaries, or at the branch points of capillaries (Attwell et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Attwell et al., 2016.

claim: More of the parallel capillaries than of the connector capillaries linking adjacent parallel capillaries received pericyte contacts (92% vs 66%, p=2.2×10−5).
source: More of the parallel capillaries than of the connector capillaries linking adjacent parallel capillaries received pericyte contacts (92% vs 66%, p=2.2×10−5, Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance.

claim: The great majority of pericytes labelled for both NG2 and PDGFRβ.
source: The great majority of pericytes labelled for both NG2 and PRGFRβ (Figure 1D)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 6.4 ± 0.2% of PDGFRβ-expressing pericytes did not express NG2 (p=2.3×10−7).
source: although a small fraction (6.4 ± 0.2%) of PDGFRβ-expressing pericytes did not express NG2 (p=2.3×10−7).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data with statistical significance.

claim: There is one pericyte every ~60 μm along rat coronary capillaries, independent of location in the left ventricle.
source: Overall there is one pericyte every ~60 μm along rat coronary capillaries, independent of location in the left ventricle (Figure 1F)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There is variability around the mean pericyte inter-soma distance.
source: Overall there is one pericyte every ~60 μm along rat coronary capillaries, independent of location in the left ventricle (Figure 1F) although there is variability around this mean distance (Figure 1A,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1A and 1G.

claim: Pericytes extend circumferential processes.
source: Pericytes extend circumferential processes (Figure 1E,G)
evidence: This claim is supported by images shown in Figures 1E and 1G.

claim: Contraction of pericyte circumferential processes would directly alter capillary diameter.
source: Pericytes extend circumferential processes (Figure 1E,G), the contraction of which would directly alter capillary diameter.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical structure of pericytes shown in the figures.

claim: Contraction of pericyte longitudinal processes could alter the stiffness of the capillary wall and regulate its deformability by passing blood cells.
source: Contraction of their longitudinal processes could alter the stiffness of the capillary wall and regulate its deformability by passing blood cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential function of longitudinal processes.

claim: Varying degrees of contraction of pericytes is a plausible explanation for the large variance of capillary blood transit time in the coronary circulation.
source: Indeed, varying degrees of contraction of these pericytes is a plausible explanation for the large variance of capillary blood transit time in the coronary circulation (Rose and Goresky, 1976)
evidence: This is an inference connecting pericyte contraction to observed transit time variance, with citation to Rose and Goresky, 1976.

claim: The large variance of capillary blood transit time has a significant effect on oxygen extraction by the myocardium.
source: Indeed, varying degrees of contraction of these pericytes is a plausible explanation for the large variance of capillary blood transit time in the coronary circulation (Rose and Goresky, 1976), which has a significant effect on oxygen extraction by the myocardium (Ostergaard et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ostergaard et al., 2014.

claim: Approximately 50% of pericytes are located close to varicosities of tyrosine hydroxylase expressing sympathetic axons.
source: We found that approximately 50% of pericytes are located close to varicosities of tyrosine hydroxylase expressing sympathetic axons (Figure 1H–J)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1H-J.

claim: The proximity of pericytes to sympathetic axons suggests the possibility of noradrenergic regulation of pericyte tone.
source: We found that approximately 50% of pericytes are located close to varicosities of tyrosine hydroxylase expressing sympathetic axons (Figure 1H–J), suggesting the possibility of noradrenergic regulation of pericyte tone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical proximity of pericytes to sympathetic axons.

claim: Pericytes are conventionally assumed to constrict capillaries using α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA).
source: Pericytes are conventionally assumed to constrict capillaries using α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA: Joyce et al., 1985; Skalli et al., 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Joyce et al., 1985 and Skalli et al., 1989.

claim: Variability in α-SMA labelling and data showing expression of other actin isoforms in pericytes has led to a suggestion that γ-actin might be the relevant actin isoform for CNS pericytes.
source: but variability in the labelling observed for α-SMA and data showing expression of other actin isoforms in pericytes has led to a suggestion, for CNS pericytes, that γ-actin might instead be the relevant actin isoform (DeNofrio et al., 1989; Grant et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeNofrio et al., 1989 and Grant et al., 2017.

claim: α-SMA labelling occurred in 36.4 ± 6.7% of 57 pericytes.
source: α-SMA labelling occurred in 36.4 ± 6.7% of 57 pericytes (Figure 1N)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: β-actin labelling occurred in 62.3 ± 2.8% of 30 pericytes.
source: and was rarer than labelling for β-actin (62.3 ± 2.8% of 30 pericytes)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data.

claim: γ-actin labelling occurred in 76.0 ± 3.4% of 47 pericytes.
source: or γ-actin (76.0 ± 3.4% of 47 pericytes).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data.

claim: α-SMA-expressing pericytes were most commonly observed in capillaries closer to the arteriole end of the capillary bed.
source: α-SMA-expressing pericytes were most commonly observed in capillaries closer to the arteriole end of the capillary bed
evidence: This is an observational claim based on the spatial distribution of α-SMA labelling.

claim: β- and γ-actin were seen in pericytes across the capillary bed.
source: while β- and γ-actin were seen in pericytes across the capillary bed.
evidence: This is an observational claim based on the spatial distribution of β- and γ-actin labelling.

claim: Occlusion of the LAD coronary artery for 45 mins deprives the anterior wall of the left ventricle and part of the right ventricle of blood.
source: To examine the possible role of contraction of pericytes in ischaemic pathology, we occluded the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery for 45 mins, depriving the anterior wall of the left ventricle and part of the right ventricle of blood (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure and its physiological effect.

claim: In control (sham LAD artery occlusion) hearts, perfusion was visible throughout the whole cross section of the left and right ventricles.
source: In control (sham LAD artery occlusion) hearts, perfusion was visible throughout the whole cross section of the left and right ventricles (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by perfusion imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The perfused blood volume per unit area was fairly uniform around the left ventricle in control hearts.
source: The perfused blood volume per unit area (assessed from the mean FITC-albumin intensity in regions of interest) was fairly uniform around the left ventricle (Figure 2C)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative perfusion data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The perfused blood volume per unit area was somewhat higher in the posterior wall of the left ventricle in control hearts.
source: The perfused blood volume per unit area (assessed from the mean FITC-albumin intensity in regions of interest) was fairly uniform around the left ventricle (Figure 2C), although somewhat higher in the posterior wall (regions of interest (ROIs) 4–6 of Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative perfusion data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Occlusion and reperfusion of the LAD artery resulted in microvascular perfusion being greatly reduced after the period of ischaemia in half of the left and right ventricles.
source: In contrast, occlusion and reperfusion of the LAD artery resulted in microvascular perfusion being greatly reduced after the period of ischaemia in half of the left and right ventricles (Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by perfusion imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After LAD occlusion and reperfusion, perfusion was reduced by 49% compared to sham-operated animals in ROIs 7–10 (p=0.0004).
source: as quantified for the left ventricle in Figure 2C (reduced by 49% compared to sham-operated animals in ROIs 7–10: p=0.0004).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative perfusion data with statistical significance shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In control hearts only 3% of capillaries were blocked in the left ventricle.
source: Higher magnification images revealed that in control hearts only 3% of capillaries were blocked (i.e. not perfused by FITC-albumin) in the left ventricle.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of high magnification perfusion images.

claim: LAD artery occlusion and reperfusion increased capillary blockage to 40% in the affected area.
source: In contrast, LAD artery occlusion and reperfusion increased this to 40% in the affected area (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of capillary blockage shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Some capillaries showed an abrupt cessation of perfusion after ischaemia and reperfusion.
source: Some capillaries were completely perfused and some were completely unperfused throughout the imaged area, while some capillaries showed an abrupt cessation of perfusion (Figure 3A–F)
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 3A-F.

claim: The abrupt cessation of perfusion occurred with a profound decrease of FITC-albumin intensity over a few microns.
source: while some capillaries showed an abrupt cessation of perfusion (Figure 3A–F), with a profound decrease of FITC-albumin intensity that occurred over a few microns (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of FITC-albumin intensity shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Leukocytes are both larger and less deformable than erythrocytes.
source: Since leukocytes are both larger and less deformable than erythrocytes (Schmid-Schönbein et al., 1981; Downey et al., 1990; Komatsu et al., 1990; Doerschuk et al., 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: No leukocytes were found lodged at 46 blockage sites examined.
source: Surprisingly, labelling with antibody to neutrophil elastase or ICAM-1 revealed no leukocytes lodged at 46 blockage sites examined
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data examining blockage sites.

claim: Leukocytes were seen outside vessels, usually post-capillary venules.
source: Surprisingly, labelling with antibody to neutrophil elastase or ICAM-1 revealed no leukocytes lodged at 46 blockage sites examined (although, as a positive control, they were seen outside vessels, Figure 3K, usually post-capillary venules).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Red blood cells were associated with only 18% of 44 blockage sites.
source: Similarly, labelling for the erythrocyte protein glycophorin A revealed red blood cells (Figure 3L) associated with only a small percentage of blockage sites (18% of 44 blockages)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Even where red blood cells were trapped at capillary constrictions it did not always lead to a block of blood flow.
source: and even where red blood cells were trapped at capillary constrictions it did not always lead to a block of blood flow (as shown by FITC-albumin passing the red blood cells).
evidence: This is an observation based on the presence of FITC-albumin flow past trapped red blood cells.

claim: Many blockages occurred close to pericytes.
source: However, examining NG2 labelling at the sites of block revealed that many blockages occurred close to pericytes
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data examining blockage sites.

claim: In some cases pericyte processes appeared to visibly constrict the capillary at the block location.
source: However, examining NG2 labelling at the sites of block revealed that many blockages occurred close to pericytes, in some cases with pericyte processes appearing to visibly constrict the capillary at the block location (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 3A-C.

claim: The median distance of blockages to the nearest pericyte soma was 3.6 μm.
source: The cumulative probability distribution of this distance showed the median distance to be 3.6 μm (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: If blockages were randomly placed on the blocked capillaries, the median distance to the nearest pericyte soma would be 11.6 μm.
source: In contrast, when we used the same 42 images to calculate what the average distance of a blockage to the nearest pericyte soma would be if blockages were randomly placed on the blocked capillaries in the images (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the cumulative probability distribution for that distance predicted a median distance of 11.6 μm (Figure 3H; significantly different, p=3.9×10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical modeling and analysis shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ischaemia-evoked capillary block occurs disproportionately close to pericytes.
source: Thus, ischaemia-evoked capillary block occurs disproportionately close to pericytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analysis comparing observed and expected blockage distances from pericytes.

claim: In sham-operated animals, the ratio of capillary diameter at the pericyte soma to that upstream was 1.058 ± 0.015 (n = 20, significantly greater than one, p=0.001).
source: In sham-operated animals, the ratio of the diameter at the soma to that upstream was 1.058 ± 0.015 (n = 20, significantly greater than one, p=0.001, Figure 3I)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative diameter measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The presence of the pericyte soma induces growth of the capillary lumen in control conditions.
source: In sham-operated animals, the ratio of the diameter at the soma to that upstream was 1.058 ± 0.015 (n = 20, significantly greater than one, p=0.001, Figure 3I), consistent with the presence of the pericyte soma inducing growth of the capillary lumen, as found previously for brain pericytes (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the diameter ratio data, supported by citation to Hall et al., 2014.

claim: For capillaries after ischaemia, the ratio of diameter at the pericyte soma to that upstream was 0.822 ± 0.022 (n = 60, significantly less than control, p=1.4×10−8).
source: In contrast, for capillaries after ischaemia, this ratio was 0.822 ± 0.022 (n = 60, significantly less, p=1.4×10−8, Figure 3I)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative diameter measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The reduced diameter ratio after ischaemia implies that constriction occurs near the pericyte soma.
source: In contrast, for capillaries after ischaemia, this ratio was 0.822 ± 0.022 (n = 60, significantly less, p=1.4×10−8, Figure 3I), implying that constriction occurs near the pericyte soma.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diameter ratio data after ischaemia.

claim: The absolute diameter measured at pericyte somata was reduced by 37% after ischaemia and reperfusion compared to sham-operated hearts (p=3.1×10−6).
source: The absolute diameter measured at pericyte somata was reduced by 37% after ischaemia and reperfusion (compared to sham-operated hearts, p=3.1×10−6, Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative diameter measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 3J.

claim: All 4 pericytes near blockage sites tested for α-SMA labelling exhibited labelling.
source: Pericytes near blockage sites were tested for labelling of the different actin isoforms mentioned above. All 4 such pericytes tested for α-SMA labelling exhibited labelling (Figure 3M)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: 5 out of 6 pericytes near blockage sites tested for β-actin exhibited labelling.
source: as did 5 out of 6 tested for β-actin
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: All 6 pericytes near blockage sites tested for γ-actin exhibited labelling.
source: and all 6 tested for γ-actin.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Cardiac catecholamine transporters reverse and release noradrenaline and adrenaline in ischaemia.
source: Since cardiac catecholamine transporters reverse and release noradrenaline and adrenaline in ischaemia (Lameris et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lameris et al., 2000.

claim: Noradrenaline acts on pericytes in the brain to constrict capillaries.
source: and noradrenaline acts on pericytes in the brain to constrict capillaries (Peppiatt et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peppiatt et al., 2006.

claim: Blocking adrenergic α1 receptors with terazosin did not reduce the percentage of capillaries blocked after ischaemia.
source: We found no effect of injecting terazosin (0.5 mg/kg i.v., 5 mins before occluding the LAD artery, which produced a 20–33 mm Hg decrease of blood pressure), with 48.8 ± 3.7% of capillaries blocked in the presence of terazosin (in 13 images covering 383 capillaries in 2 hearts; not significantly different from the 44.7 ± 4.9% seen for 14 images covering 366 capillaries in 2 hearts in interleaved experiments without terazosin, p=0.52).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing terazosin-treated and control conditions.

claim: Adenosine has been suggested to reduce no-reflow after cardiac ischaemia, although its clinical utility remains uncertain.
source: Adenosine has been suggested to reduce no-reflow after cardiac ischaemia, although its clinical utility remains uncertain (Berg and Buhari, 2012; Su et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berg and Buhari, 2012 and Su et al., 2015.

claim: Adenosine is thought to relax pericytes.
source: Adenosine is also thought to relax pericytes (Matsugi et al., 1997; Li and Puro, 2001; Gaudin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matsugi et al., 1997, Li and Puro, 2001, and Gaudin et al., 2014.

claim: Adenosine significantly reduced the decrease of coronary perfusion seen after ischaemia (p=0.03).
source: Adenosine significantly reduced (p=0.03) the decrease of coronary perfusion seen after ischaemia (Figure 2C
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative perfusion data with statistical significance shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adenosine increased the mean perfusion value in ROIs 7–10 by 57% compared to ischaemia without adenosine.
source: the mean value in ROIs 7–10 in Figure 2C was increased by 57% compared to ischaemia without adenosine
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative perfusion data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: With adenosine treatment, perfusion after ischaemia was not significantly different from control conditions (p=0.77).
source: and was not significantly different from that in control conditions, p=0.77).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of perfusion data.

claim: Adenosine reduced by one quarter the percentage of capillaries that were blocked after reperfusion, from ~40% to ~30% (p=0.007).
source: However, adenosine also reduced by one quarter the percentage of capillaries that were blocked after reperfusion, from ~40% to ~30% (p=0.007, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative capillary blockage data with statistical significance shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The remaining sites of block after adenosine treatment were still significantly associated with pericyte locations (p=0.001).
source: An analysis like that in Figure 3H showed that the remaining sites of block were still significantly associated with pericyte locations (p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of blockage locations relative to pericytes.

claim: Adenosine significantly reduced the constriction evoked by ischaemia at pericyte somata (p=0.0045).
source: To test this hypothesis, we compared the diameter of capillaries at pericyte somata with the diameter 10 μm upstream of the soma and found that adenosine significantly (p=0.0045) reduced the constriction evoked by ischaemia at pericyte somata (Figure 3I)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative diameter measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Adenosine's reduction of constriction at pericyte somata implies a specific effect on pericytes rather than a general capillary dilation produced by upstream arteriole dilation.
source: we compared the diameter of capillaries at pericyte somata with the diameter 10 μm upstream of the soma and found that adenosine significantly (p=0.0045) reduced the constriction evoked by ischaemia at pericyte somata (Figure 3I), implying a specific effect on pericytes (rather than a general capillary dilation produced by upstream arteriole dilation).
evidence: This is an inference based on the specific location of diameter changes at pericyte somata.

claim: The absolute capillary diameter at pericyte somata after ischaemia was increased by 21% using adenosine (p=0.025).
source: The absolute capillary diameter at pericyte somata after ischaemia was increased by 21% using adenosine (p=0.025, Figure 3J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative diameter measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Adenosine decreases no-reflow by relaxing pericytes.
source: Thus, adenosine decreases no-reflow by relaxing pericytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined evidence of adenosine's effects on capillary diameter at pericyte locations and reduction of blockages.

claim: During ischaemia pericytes constrict and block coronary capillaries, probably because pericyte [Ca2+]i rises when ion pumping stops in ischaemia.
source: Our data suggest a novel therapeutic target for reducing no-reflow after cardiac ischaemia: during ischaemia pericytes constrict and block coronary capillaries, probably because pericyte [Ca2+]i rises when ion pumping stops in ischaemia.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the experimental data and knowledge of cellular physiology during ischaemia.

claim: Cardiac pericytes extend actomyosin-containing processes around coronary capillaries that reduce capillary diameter when their [Ca2+]i rises and contraction is activated.
source: The most plausible explanation of our data is that, like pericytes in the CNS (Peppiatt et al., 2006; Hall et al., 2014), cardiac pericytes extend actomyosin-containing processes around coronary capillaries that, when their [Ca2+]i rises and contraction is activated, reduce capillary diameter (see Supplementary Movie 1 of Peppiatt et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison with CNS pericytes, supported by citations.

claim: Cardiac pericytes express both actin and myosin.
source: Indeed, cardiac pericytes express both actin and myosin (Joyce et al., 1985; Skalli et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Joyce et al., 1985 and Skalli et al., 1989.

claim: Pericytes do not need to completely constrict a capillary in order to stop blood flow in that vessel.
source: It is likely that pericytes do not need to completely constrict a capillary in order to stop blood flow in that vessel
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that partial constriction can prevent cell passage.

claim: A reduction in capillary diameter may prevent the passage of leukocytes or red blood cells, causing a blockage that prevents the passage of both plasma and cells.
source: because a reduction in diameter (like the 37% in Figure 3J) may prevent the passage of leukocytes (Engler et al., 1983) or red blood cells (Figure 3L), causing a blockage that prevents the passage of both plasma and cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diameter reduction data and citation to Engler et al., 1983, plus observation of trapped red blood cells.

claim: The observation of few cells in the capillary lumen at blockages may result from their displacement during the perfusion with FITC-albumin in gelatin.
source: The fact that we observed few cells in the capillary lumen at blockages may result from their displacement during the perfusion with FITC-albumin in gelatin
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation of few cells at blockage sites.

claim: Capillary block may occur when constriction brings together the layers of glycocalyx on opposite sides of the capillary.
source: or may alternatively reflect capillary block occurring when constriction brings together the layers of glycocalyx (Secomb et al., 1998) on opposite sides of the capillary.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for capillary block, supported by citation to Secomb et al., 1998.

claim: Not all pericytes die during the 45 min period of ischaemia used in this study.
source: Clearly not all pericytes die during the 45 min period of ischaemia used here (which in severe brain ischaemia kills ~50% of pericytes: Hall et al., 2014) because, if they did, then adenosine applied around the time of reperfusion would not be able to reduce the amount of capillary constriction and block occurring.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effectiveness of adenosine treatment, with citation to Hall et al., 2014 for comparison.

claim: Adenosine would produce a greater restoration of flow if pericyte death were prevented.
source: However, adenosine only reduces the number of blocked capillaries by 25% (Figure 3J) and conceivably it would produce a greater restoration of flow if pericyte death were prevented.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential improvements to adenosine treatment.

claim: At short times after ischaemia, constriction of downstream capillary pericytes is expected to occur also in human cardiac tissue.
source: Nevertheless, at short times after ischaemia, we expect the constriction that we observe of downstream capillary pericytes to occur also in human cardiac tissue, prolonging the period of ischaemia.
evidence: This is an inference extrapolating from the rat model to human tissue.

claim: Ischaemia selectively reduces capillary diameter near pericytes.
source: Our demonstration that ischaemia selectively reduces capillary diameter near pericytes suggests that, at least at early times, the majority of capillary blockages in fact occur near pericytes that have constricted the capillaries.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diameter measurements at pericyte locations.

claim: At least at early times, the majority of capillary blockages occur near pericytes that have constricted the capillaries.
source: Our demonstration that ischaemia selectively reduces capillary diameter near pericytes suggests that, at least at early times, the majority of capillary blockages in fact occur near pericytes that have constricted the capillaries.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial association of blockages with pericytes and diameter reduction at pericyte locations.

claim: Pericytes are a novel drug target for treating the coronary no-reflow that often occurs after primary percutaneous coronary intervention.
source: These data imply that pericytes are a novel drug target for treating the coronary no-reflow that often occurs after primary percutaneous coronary intervention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about pericyte involvement in no-reflow.

claim: Deletion of pericyte-capillary interactions mediated by the angiopoietin/TIE and PDGF/PDGFRβ pathways may affect the contractile properties of pericytes and their response to ischaemia.
source: It would be interesting to test whether deletion of pericyte-capillary interactions mediated by the angiopoietin/TIE and PDGF/PDGFRβ pathways (Ziegler et al., 2013) affect the contractile properties of pericytes and their response to ischaemia.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future research, with citation to Ziegler et al., 2013.

claim: Adenosine may act on arteriolar smooth muscle and lower blood pressure.
source: We used adenosine to relax pericytes (an effect verified from measurements of capillary diameter at pericyte locations in Figure 3I–J), but it may also act on arteriolar smooth muscle and lower blood pressure.
evidence: This is an inference about additional effects of adenosine beyond pericyte relaxation.

claim: To reduce no-reflow therapeutically by preventing pericyte constriction of coronary capillaries, it will be necessary to develop agents that act selectively on pericytes.
source: To reduce no-reflow therapeutically by preventing pericyte constriction of coronary capillaries, it will be necessary to develop agents that act selectively on pericytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the need for selective therapeutic agents based on the findings.

claim: In the brain, signalling pathways regulating pericyte constriction can differ from those regulating arteriole smooth muscle.
source: Encouragingly, in the brain it has been shown that signalling pathways regulating pericyte constriction can differ from those regulating arteriole smooth muscle (Mishra et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mishra et al., 2016.

claim: Other organs susceptible to ischaemic no-reflow pathology, such as the kidneys, muscle and skin, may also be damaged by a pericyte-mediated mechanism.
source: Our data also raise the possibility that other organs susceptible to ischaemic no-reflow pathology, such as the kidneys, muscle and skin, may also be damaged by a pericyte-mediated mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation of the findings to other organs.

claim: Noradrenaline release may regulate coronary blood flow at the capillary level in physiological conditions.
source: Finally, given the proximity of cardiac pericytes to sympathetic terminals (Figure 1H–J), noradrenaline release may also regulate coronary blood flow at the capillary level in physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the anatomical proximity of pericytes to sympathetic terminals.

claim: Occlusion of a rat coronary artery, followed by reperfusion, blocks 40% of cardiac capillaries.
source: We now show that occlusion of a rat coronary artery, followed by reperfusion, blocks 40% of cardiac capillaries
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on capillary blockage after ischaemia-reperfusion.

claim: Occlusion of a rat coronary artery, followed by reperfusion, halves perfused blood volume within the affected region.
source: We now show that occlusion of a rat coronary artery, followed by reperfusion, blocks 40% of cardiac capillaries and halves perfused blood volume within the affected region.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental perfusion data.

claim: Capillary blockages colocalised strongly with pericytes.
source: Capillary blockages colocalised strongly with pericytes
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial analysis of blockage locations relative to pericytes.

claim: Capillary diameter was reduced by 37% at pericyte locations after ischaemia-reperfusion.
source: where capillary diameter was reduced by 37%.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative diameter measurements.

claim: The pericyte relaxant adenosine increased capillary diameter by 21% at pericyte somata.
source: The pericyte relaxant adenosine increased capillary diameter by 21% at pericyte somata
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative diameter measurements with adenosine treatment.

claim: Adenosine decreased capillary block by 25%.
source: decreased capillary block by 25%
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of capillary blockage with adenosine treatment.

claim: Adenosine increased perfusion volume by 57%.
source: and increased perfusion volume by 57%.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative perfusion measurements with adenosine treatment.

claim: Cardiac pericytes constrict coronary capillaries and reduce microvascular blood flow after ischaemia, despite re-opening of the culprit artery.
source: Thus, cardiac pericytes constrict coronary capillaries and reduce microvascular blood flow after ischaemia, despite re-opening of the culprit artery.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental evidence.

claim: Cardiac pericytes are a novel therapeutic target in ischaemic heart disease.
source: Cardiac pericytes are therefore a novel therapeutic target in ischaemic heart disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings about pericyte involvement in no-reflow.

claim: Ischaemia-induced constriction of coronary capillaries by pericytes contributes to no-reflow after cardiac ischaemia.
source: Here we show that ischaemia-induced constriction of coronary capillaries by pericytes contributes to no-reflow after cardiac ischaemia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental evidence.
